paragraphs: §1 — The argument from the unity of the transmission chain

The matter of these people and their position is easy indeed, the effort against them slight, and the argument against them requires no exertion or extra labor. For they have affirmed something and denied something equivalent to it, with no difference between the two — since the proof for what they deny is the same as the proof for what they affirm.

Namely: those who transmitted the report of Moses and Joshua (יהושוע) — by whom the Samaritans' own case is established — are the same people who, in their entirety, transmitted the reports of all the prophets who came after the two of them. So if, in their transmission of the reports of those who came after Joshua, they are not in the right and the transmission is not sound, then by the same token their transmission of the report of Moses and Joshua and of those two prophets' books is not in the right and not sound either. And if their transmission of the report of Moses and Joshua and of their two books is sound — without doubt or uncertainty, returning to a reliable basis and establishing the truth — then likewise their transmission of the report of those who came after the two, and of their books, is a sound transmission by which the case is established. To depart from this is self-contradiction.

If they distinguish between the two reports and make the criterion of distinction their own departure from one of them and their adherence to the other, then it must follow that if any community at all departs from the religion of Moses and denies his prophethood, that departure annuls his case [too]. And this is the height of absurdity — since a sound transmission, which compels knowledge, is not annulled by the departure of whoever has departed from it,

[p315] just as a corrupt and weak report is not made sound by the entry of whoever has entered into it, when the original report did not come from a people whose accounts yield knowledge and establish the case. This argument has applications elsewhere, and we shall pursue it exhaustively in its proper place.
§2 — They are Cuthites, not Israelites

Among the things that invalidate their claim — whether the claim that they were among the transmitters [of the Mosaic religion], or alternatively that they stand outside the transmission — is this: they are a people who entered into the worship of the Torah at a time close to the cessation of the kingdom and the state, according to what has already been said: that they are the Cuthites (הַכּוּתִים) who were brought into the religion after the exile of the Ten Tribes. As for their denying this and claiming to be from the Children of Israel, the consensus and the transmission whose foundation is upon the [scriptural] text — a transmission of the very mode as the transmission of the Torah — gives the lie to that claim.
§3 — The niddah-hut and the Cuthites among them

What further reinforces their lie in this is the matter of the Cuthites (הַכּוּתִים) who are among them and with them — that the Samaritans do not marry from them. And what confirms it still more is that they construct a "niddah" (נִדָּה) [seclusion-hut], which none of them enters; only the Cuthites alone are set apart for it and to sit in it. When they are asked why they themselves abstain from it, they answer, "Thus we have transmitted." Yet can any doubter doubt that this transmission of theirs is built upon the scriptural verse: "[Whoever] touches him [the corpse]… every native of Israel shall dwell in tabernacles" (נוּקִי יִגַּע מִבּוֹ כָּל הָאֹרֵחַ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשֵׁבוּ בַּסֻּכּוֹת)?

: The Hebrew as transcribed appears to splice corpse-impurity language (cf. Num 19:11) with the sukkot command of Lev 23:42 ("every native of Israel shall dwell in sukkot"). Q's polemical point is that the Samaritan niddah-hut practice rests on a misappropriated proof-text. The OCR reading is uncertain; verify against the JPG before quoting.
§4 — Praying toward Gerizim follows from their denial of later prophets

As for their facing in prayer toward Shechem (שְׁכֶם) and Mount Gerizim (הַר גְּרִיזִים), this corresponds to their denial of all the prophets who came after Joshua (יְהוֹשֻׁעַ) — since the facing of the [Jerusalem] Temple and its construction only came after [Joshua]. Once what they deny among the prophets is invalidated and the prophets' prophethood is established, their position in this matter falls, and facing Jerusalem in prayer becomes obligatory. We shall set this out in its place when treating prayer.
§5 — On the Second Temple [fragmentary]

Among what further reinforces their lie and the burden they carry: that the first [...] which is mentioned among them [...] their books which they read [...]; the Second Temple — he [Zerubbabel?] and his companions ask [...] entry into [...] but they did not [...] in invalidating [...] and that Jerusalem has no [...] its details [...] nor is it necessary that [...] nor the resolving toward it. So why did they ask to be among those who would build it, and not [...] against them
[p314] when [...]. Perhaps what led them to deviate from it [the building of the Second Temple] was this very episode.

: This section is heavily fragmented on the printed page; OCR could only recover scattered phrases. The argument appears to be that the Samaritans tried to participate in the Second Temple project (cf. Ezra 4) but were rebuffed, and their later anti-Jerusalem stance is a back-formation from that rejection.
§6 — Their reading of the Torah ("the stammering tongue")

Another thing that adds clarity to the frailty of their case, the corruption of their position, and their being at variance with the religion, is their reading of the Torah at variance with the way it is read by the whole community from East to West — that which the Rabbanites call "the stammering tongue" (לשון ועלג) — together with what we have mentioned of the additions and omissions they employ. Is it conceivable that the whole community has been heedless (?) or has intentionally altered [the text], while they — a small group, a coarse handful — have stood upon what is correct? This cannot be; and the book's [argument] against them [needs no elaboration]; the corruption [of their position] is plain even to a child, let alone to others. Were it not that I wished to omit nothing of what is needed in the book, I would not have mentioned even what I have mentioned.
§7 — Their denial of resurrection, deferred

As for the denial of resurrection (المعاد) by one of their two factions: we shall treat resurrection when discussing the Christians, and shall also address [there] their claim that the Torah does not mention reward and punishment.
§8 — The objection from the priestly teacher, and its answer

Now perhaps a questioner may ask: "If the Samaritans existed in the era of prophecy, and the one who taught them the religion was one of the priests who had been exiled, then their school must be sound and what they hold must be true — since that priest can only have taught them the sound religion."

We answer: this would only have to be the case if the community at that time had been standing upon the truth and obedience. But how, when the very reason they were exiled was their abandonment of the truth and their persistence in falsehood? This is what we have already said: that they were exiled while standing upon the schools of Jeroboam (ירבעם). The priest who taught them the religion only taught them according to what he and others had adopted from those schools.

This is further confirmed by the Samaritans' establishing the months upon a "high place" (במה) of their own, other than the Jerusalem Temple (בית המקדש); and the origin of that comes from Jeroboam (ירבעם), as Scripture says concerning him: [p313 top] "like Jeroboam son of Nebat, who sinned and caused [Israel] to sin" (כְּמָא יִרְבְעָם בֶּן־נְבָט אֲשֶׁר חָטָא וְהֶחֱטִיא) — and that upon a thing he himself invented and made into a custom (?).
: Variant of the formulaic refrain in Kings (e.g. 1 Kgs 14:16; 15:30, 34; 16:19, 26; 2 Kgs 3:3), where Jeroboam is repeatedly named as the archetype of those who "sinned and caused Israel to sin."
It is also possible that the [priest] still living who taught them was himself from Jeroboam's followers, whom he had selected from among the community.
§9 — Objection: if both Rabbanites and Samaritans trace to Jeroboam, why the difference?

If someone says: "If what the [Rabbanite] community holds traces back, at its root, to Jeroboam and his people — and likewise the Samaritans — then there should not be disagreement between them. But we see great disagreement between them, and this undermines your premise."

We answer: even granting that the root of both is from a single place, each of the two parties has, since that time, undergone alterations, additions, and subtractions. The Rabbanites, when they took over the community, changed certain things from what the community had held, added some things to the schools of Jeroboam, and subtracted others — so that the leadership might be theirs. Likewise it is possible that the Samaritans had leaders set over them — like Dustai (?) (הדוסא) and others — who did the same. If so, the objection falls and it does not follow that the Samaritans are in the right, nor that they are transmitters; just as it does not follow that the Rabbanites are in the right or transmitters. Indeed the Samaritans' case is feebler and weaker than that of the Rabbanites — since the great majority of the community adopts the schools of the Rabbanites, while the Samaritans are only a small remnant, paid no attention to and given no weight.

Let us now follow what we have said with a refutation of the Christians — who, at their root, are simply a faction that split off from the Jews, and whose case ultimately led them to a belief in ilḥād (heresy / unbelief) while still claiming monotheism.

- Samaritans (السامرة): Q follows the standard medieval Jewish identification of the Samaritans with the Kuthim of 2 Kgs 17, an Assyrian-resettled people who took up a corrupt form of Israelite religion — not authentic descendants of the Northern tribes. This argument was a commonplace in both Rabbanite and Karaite anti-Samaritan polemic.

- "The stammering tongue" (לשון ועלג): A Rabbanite slur for the Samaritan Hebrew pronunciation, drawing on Isa 28:11 ("with a stammering of the lip"). Q cites it approvingly as evidence that Samaritan readings of the Torah are textually corrupt.

- §5 fragmentation: The argument from Second Temple history (Samaritan exclusion from the rebuilding) is conventional anti-Samaritan material in this period; the lost or OCR-corrupt portions can probably be reconstructed by reference to Ezra 4 traditions. Verify against the JPG of p315 before publication.
- דוסא / הדוסא (§9): A Samaritan or proto-Samaritan figure. Possibly Dosa b. Yannai (a high priest in some Samaritan chronologies) or a corruption of another name.

- ilḥād (الحاد, §9): Q uses this loaded Islamic term — usually rendered "heresy" or "atheism" — for the Christian doctrinal position. The sting is that Christians "claim monotheism" (التوحيد) but in fact deny it (in his view). This sets up the long Christian critique that runs through babs 2–6.
